dmm-2015-power-01c.title: Run the algorithm
dmm-2015-power-01c.body:
$x_0=\sqrt3=1+(\sqrt3-1)$, so $a_0=1$. $x_1=\frac1{\sqrt3-1}=\frac{\sqrt3+1}2=1+\frac{\sqrt3-1}2$, so $a_1=1$. $x_2=\frac2{\sqrt3-1}=\sqrt3+1=2+(\sqrt3-1)$, so $a_2=2$, and the remainder $\sqrt3-1$ is the same as after the first step, so $x_3=x_1$ and the pattern repeats: $\sqrt3=[1,1,2,1,2,\dots]=[1,\overline{1,2}]$.

**Answer: $[1,\overline{1,2}]$**

dmm-2015-power-01d.title: Solve for the periodic part
dmm-2015-power-01d.body:
Let $x=[\overline{2,4}]=2+\cfrac1{4+\cfrac1x}$. Then $x=2+\frac{x}{4x+1}=\frac{9x+2}{4x+1}$, so $4x^2+x=9x+2$, i.e. $2x^2-4x-1=0$ and $x=\frac{2+\sqrt6}2$ (the positive root). Hence $[2,\overline{2,4}]=2+\frac1x=2+\frac2{2+\sqrt6}=2+(\sqrt6-2)=\sqrt6$.

**Answer: $\sqrt6$**

dmm-2015-power-02b.title: Expand with the recurrence
dmm-2015-power-02b.body: $p_nq_{n-2}-p_{n-2}q_n=(a_np_{n-1}+p_{n-2})q_{n-2}-p_{n-2}(a_nq_{n-1}+q_{n-2})=a_n(p_{n-1}q_{n-2}-p_{n-2}q_{n-1})=a_n(-1)^{n-2}=(-1)^na_n$, using part (a) with $n-1$ in place of $n$. $\blacksquare$

dmm-2015-power-03.title: All partial quotients are 1
dmm-2015-power-03.body: Let $\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2$; then $\varphi^2=\varphi+1$, so $\varphi=1+\frac1\varphi$. Hence $x_0=\varphi$ has $a_0=1$ and $x_1=\frac1{\varphi-1}=\varphi$ again, so every $a_i=1$ and $\varphi=[1,1,1,\dots]$. By Theorem 1, $p_0=1,p_1=2$ and $p_n=p_{n-1}+p_{n-2}$; $q_0=1,q_1=1$ and $q_n=q_{n-1}+q_{n-2}$. Comparing with $F_1=1,F_2=2$ and $F_0=F_1=1$ gives $p_n=F_{n+1}$ and $q_n=F_n$. So the $(n+1)$-th convergent $\frac{p_n}{q_n}$ is $\frac{F_{n+1}}{F_n}$, i.e. the $N$-th convergent is $\frac{F_N}{F_{N-1}}$. $\blacksquare$

dmm-2015-power-05a.title: Between two consecutive convergents
dmm-2015-power-05a.body: By Theorem 2, $\alpha$ lies strictly between $\frac{p_n}{q_n}$ and $\frac{p_{n+1}}{q_{n+1}}$ (one is below, the other above $\alpha$). Hence $\left|\alpha-\frac{p_n}{q_n}\right|<\left|\frac{p_{n+1}}{q_{n+1}}-\frac{p_n}{q_n}\right|=\frac{|p_{n+1}q_n-p_nq_{n+1}|}{q_nq_{n+1}}=\frac1{q_nq_{n+1}}$. $\blacksquare$

dmm-2015-power-05b.title: AM-GM
dmm-2015-power-05b.body: Suppose neither satisfies the inequality: $\left|\alpha-\frac{p_n}{q_n}\right|\ge\frac1{2q_n^2}$ and $\left|\alpha-\frac{p_{n+1}}{q_{n+1}}\right|\ge\frac1{2q_{n+1}^2}$. Since $\alpha$ lies between the two convergents, the two distances add up to $\left|\frac{p_{n+1}}{q_{n+1}}-\frac{p_n}{q_n}\right|=\frac1{q_nq_{n+1}}$. Therefore $$\frac1{q_nq_{n+1}}\ge\frac1{2q_n^2}+\frac1{2q_{n+1}^2}\ge\frac1{q_nq_{n+1}},$$ the last step by AM-GM. So equality holds throughout: both distances are exactly $\frac1{2q^2}$ and $q_n=q_{n+1}=q$, which makes $\alpha$ the midpoint $\frac{p_n+p_{n+1}}{2q}$ of the two convergents, a rational number. This contradicts the irrationality of $\alpha$. $\blacksquare$

dmm-2015-power-05c.title: Convergents of the square root of 2
dmm-2015-power-05c.body:
$\sqrt2=1+(\sqrt2-1)$ and $\frac1{\sqrt2-1}=\sqrt2+1=2+(\sqrt2-1)$, so $\sqrt2=[1,2,2,2,\dots]$. By Theorem 1: $p_n=1,3,7,17,41,99,\dots$ and $q_n=1,2,5,12,29,70,\dots$. Since $\left|\sqrt2-\frac{41}{29}\right|<\frac1{29\cdot70}=\frac1{2030}<\frac1{1000}$, the fraction $\frac{41}{29}$ works (so does $\frac{99}{70}$).

**Answer: $\frac{41}{29}$**

dmm-2015-power-06a.title: Signs and sizes
dmm-2015-power-06a.body: $\alpha-\alpha'=\frac{2\sqrt D}{Q}>0$ (as $\alpha>1>0>\alpha'$), so $Q>0$. Since $\alpha>1$ and $\alpha'>-1$ we get $\alpha+\alpha'=\frac{2P}Q>0$, so $P>0$. From $\alpha'=\frac{P-\sqrt D}Q<0$: $P<\sqrt D$. From $\alpha>1$: $Q<P+\sqrt D<2\sqrt D$. $\blacksquare$

dmm-2015-power-06b.title: Check the three conditions
dmm-2015-power-06b.body: Let $q=\lfloor\alpha\rfloor\ge1$, so $\alpha_1=\frac1{\alpha-q}$. *Quadratic irrational:* $\alpha-q=\frac{A+\sqrt D}{Q}$ with $A=P-qQ$, so $\alpha_1=\frac{Q}{A+\sqrt D}=\frac{Q(\sqrt D-A)}{D-A^2}=\frac{-AQ+\sqrt{Q^2D}}{D-A^2}$ has the required form (and $D-A^2\ne0$, $Q^2D$ is not a square). *$\alpha_1>1$:* $0<\alpha-q<1$ because $\alpha$ is irrational. *Conjugate:* taking conjugates in $\alpha=q+\frac1{\alpha_1}$ (conjugation respects sums and products, hence reciprocals) gives $\alpha'=q+\frac1{\alpha_1'}$, so $\alpha_1'=\frac1{\alpha'-q}$. Now $\alpha'<0$ and $q\ge1$ give $\alpha'-q<-1$, so $-1<\alpha_1'<0$. Hence $\alpha_1$ is reduced. $\blacksquare$

dmm-2015-power-06c.title: Pigeonhole
dmm-2015-power-06c.body: Write $\alpha=\frac{P+\sqrt D}Q$ with $Q\mid D-P^2$ (always possible: multiply numerator and denominator by $|Q|$). If $\alpha_i=\frac{P_i+\sqrt D}{Q_i}$ with $Q_i\mid D-P_i^2$ and $q_i=\lfloor\alpha_i\rfloor$, put $A=P_i-q_iQ_i$; then $\alpha_{i+1}=\frac1{\alpha_i-q_i}=\frac{Q_i}{A+\sqrt D}=\frac{-A+\sqrt D}{Q_{i+1}}$ with $Q_{i+1}=\frac{D-A^2}{Q_i}$, an integer because $D-A^2\equiv D-P_i^2\equiv0\pmod{Q_i}$; and $Q_{i+1}\mid D-A^2$. So each $\alpha_i=\frac{P_i+\sqrt D}{Q_i}$ has the same $D$ and integer $P_i,Q_i$. By (b) every $\alpha_i$ is reduced, so by (a) $0<P_i<\sqrt D$ and $0<Q_i<2\sqrt D$. There are only finitely many such pairs $(P_i,Q_i)$, so $\alpha_i=\alpha_j$ for some $i<j$. Since $\alpha_{k+1}=\frac1{\alpha_k-\lfloor\alpha_k\rfloor}$ is determined by $\alpha_k$, it follows that $\alpha_{i+k}=\alpha_{j+k}$ for all $k\ge0$: the sequence is periodic from $i$ on with period $l=j-i$. $\blacksquare$

dmm-2015-power-07a.title: Conditions for reduced
dmm-2015-power-07a.body: We need $\sqrt N+m>1$ and $-1<m-\sqrt N<0$ (the conjugate of $\sqrt N+m$ is $m-\sqrt N$). The second says $\sqrt N-1<m<\sqrt N$; since $\sqrt N$ is not an integer, $m=\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor$ satisfies it. Then $m\ge1$ gives $\sqrt N+m>1$. So $m=\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor$. $\blacksquare$

dmm-2015-power-07b.title: Subtract m
dmm-2015-power-07b.body: With $m=\lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor$, the number $\sqrt N+m$ is reduced, so by Theorem 3 it is purely periodic: $\sqrt N+m=[\overline{b_0,b_1,\dots,b_n}]$ where $b_0=\lfloor\sqrt N+m\rfloor=2m$. Thus $\sqrt N+m=[2m,b_1,\dots,b_n,2m,b_1,\dots]$, and subtracting $m$ from the integer part, $\sqrt N=[m,b_1,\dots,b_n,2m,b_1,\dots,b_n,2m,\dots]=[a_0,\overline{a_1,\dots,a_n,2a_0}]$ with $a_0=m$ and $a_i=b_i$. $\blacksquare$

dmm-2015-power-08a.title: Pick's theorem
dmm-2015-power-08a.body: The area is $\frac12|P_{n+2}Q_n-P_nQ_{n+2}|=\frac{a_{n+2}}2$. Boundary points: since $(P_{n+2},Q_{n+2})=(P_n,Q_n)+a_{n+2}(P_{n+1},Q_{n+1})$ and $\gcd(P_{n+1},Q_{n+1})=1$ (from $P_{n+1}Q_n-P_nQ_{n+1}=\pm1$), the side between $(P_n,Q_n)$ and $(P_{n+2},Q_{n+2})$ contains exactly the $a_{n+2}+1$ lattice points $(P_n,Q_n)+i(P_{n+1},Q_{n+1})$, $0\le i\le a_{n+2}$. The other two sides contain no further lattice points because $\gcd(P_n,Q_n)=\gcd(P_{n+2},Q_{n+2})=1$. Together with the origin, $B=a_{n+2}+2$. Pick's theorem gives $\frac{a_{n+2}}2=I+\frac{a_{n+2}+2}2-1=I+\frac{a_{n+2}}2$, so $I=0$. $\blacksquare$

dmm-2015-power-08b.title: Area comparison
dmm-2015-power-08b.body:
Call the parallelogram $\Pi$, with vertices $O=(0,0)$, $U=(2Q\alpha,2Q)$, $W=(2P,2Q)$, $V=(2P-2Q\alpha,0)$ and centre $C=(P,Q)$. Its area is $\left|\det\begin{pmatrix}2Q\alpha&2P-2Q\alpha\\2Q&0\end{pmatrix}\right|=4Q|P-Q\alpha|=4Q^2\left|\alpha-\frac PQ\right|<2$.

Suppose a lattice point $X\neq C$ lies in the interior of $\Pi$. Then $X'=2C-X$ (its reflection in the centre) is also an interior lattice point. The interior points of $\Pi$ on the diagonal $OW$ form the open segment from $O$ to $W=2C$, whose only lattice point is $C$ (as $\gcd(P,Q)=1$); so $X$ is not on line $OW$ and $\det(X,C)\ne0$, i.e. $|\det(X,C)|\ge1$. The quadrilateral $OXWX'$ has diagonals $OW$ and $XX'$ bisecting each other at $C$, so it is a parallelogram; it lies in $\Pi$ (convexity) and has area $|\det(X,W)|=2|\det(X,C)|\ge2$. This contradicts area$(\Pi)<2$. $\blacksquare$

dmm-2015-power-08c.title: Algebraic proof
dmm-2015-power-08c.body:
Put $p_{-1}=1,q_{-1}=0$ so that the recurrences hold for all $n\ge0$. Expand $\frac PQ=[a_0,\dots,a_n]$ (a finite expansion, with $a_n\ge1$). Since $[\dots,a_n]=[\dots,a_n-1,1]$ (for $a_n\ge2$) and $[\dots,a_{n-1},1]=[\dots,a_{n-1}+1]$, we may choose the parity of $n$ freely. As $\gcd(P,Q)=1$ and the $q_k$ are positive, $p_n=P$, $q_n=Q$. Write $\alpha-\frac PQ=\frac{(-1)^n\theta}{Q^2}$; choose the parity of $n$ so that $\theta>0$, then $0<\theta<\frac12$.

Define $\omega$ by $\alpha=\frac{\omega p_n+p_{n-1}}{\omega q_n+q_{n-1}}$. Then
$$\alpha-\frac{p_n}{q_n}=\frac{p_{n-1}q_n-p_nq_{n-1}}{q_n(\omega q_n+q_{n-1})}=\frac{(-1)^n}{q_n(\omega q_n+q_{n-1})}$$
by part 2(a). Comparing with $\frac{(-1)^n\theta}{q_n^2}$ gives $\omega q_n+q_{n-1}=\frac{q_n}\theta$, so $\omega=\frac1\theta-\frac{q_{n-1}}{q_n}>2-1=1$ (as $q_{n-1}\le q_n$). Now $\omega$ is irrational and $>1$, so it has an infinite expansion $\omega=[b_0,b_1,\dots]$ with all $b_i\ge1$, and $\alpha=\frac{\omega p_n+p_{n-1}}{\omega q_n+q_{n-1}}=[a_0,\dots,a_n,b_0,b_1,\dots]$. This is an expansion of $\alpha$ with positive partial quotients after $a_0$, hence it is *the* expansion of $\alpha$ produced by the algorithm, and its $n$-th convergent is $\frac{p_n}{q_n}=\frac PQ$. $\blacksquare$
